blocks.content: Identify wire types/insulation and selection factors.

items.definition: PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, brand name Teflon) insulated wire, designated MIL-W-22759 series, is the most common wire insulation in modern GA aircraft. It offers excellent temperature resistance (-65°C to +200°C), light weight, low dielectric loss, and chemical/abrasion resistance.
items.analogy: PTFE wire is the non-stick pan of aircraft wiring — nothing sticks to it (chemicals slide off), it handles high heat, and it's durable under harsh conditions.

items.definition: Near aircraft engines and other high-temperature zones, MIL-W-22759/16 (PTFE/Teflon-insulated, rated to ~200°C) or fiberglass-insulated wire is required; standard PVC or nylon-insulated wire cannot withstand engine bay temperatures.
items.analogy: Using standard wire near an aircraft engine is like using a regular plastic bag next to an oven — it will melt. You need a heat-rated container (PTFE or fiberglass wire) for the heat zone.

items.definition: Wire insulation must be matched to its installation environment on three criteria: temperature rating (must exceed maximum local temperature), chemical resistance (must resist fluids present — fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid), and abrasion resistance (must withstand routing conditions — conduit, structure contact).
items.analogy: Choosing wire insulation is like selecting outdoor clothing — match the material to the weather (temperature), terrain (abrasion), and potential wet conditions (chemical resistance). One-size-fits-all doesn't work.

items.definition: PTFE (Teflon) insulation is thin and tightly bonded to the conductor. Automatic strippers must have the blade depth precisely set for the wire gauge — too deep nicks the conductor (structural weakness), too shallow leaves insulation residue (insulation contamination of the connection).
items.analogy: Stripping Teflon wire is like peeling a thin-skinned fruit with a sharp knife — set the blade too deep and you cut into the flesh (conductor); too shallow and you leave peel (insulation) behind.

blocks.question: What type of wire insulation is most commonly used in modern general aviation aircraft?
choices: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) insulation — low cost and widely available
PTFE (Teflon) or MIL-W-22759 series — light weight, temperature resistant, and durable
Rubber insulation — flexible and impact resistant
Fiberglass insulation — used for highest temperature applications only
blocks.feedback: PTFE (Teflon) wire per MIL-W-22759 is the industry standard for modern GA aircraft. PVC and rubber are too heavy and have limited temperature ranges. Fiberglass is for extreme heat zones only.

blocks.question: What type of wire insulation is required in high-temperature areas near aircraft engines?
choices: High-temperature wire such as PTFE (MIL-W-22759/16) or fiberglass-insulated wire
Nylon-jacketed wire with a temperature rating of 80°C
Rubber-insulated wire with a braided cotton outer jacket
blocks.feedback: Engine bay temperatures can exceed 150°C or more. Only high-temperature insulations (PTFE at ~200°C, fiberglass at 400°C+) are suitable. PVC, nylon, and rubber insulations would melt or degrade.

blocks.question: What is the primary consideration when selecting wire insulation material for an aircraft installation?
choices: Selecting the insulation with the lowest dielectric constant to minimize signal loss
Choosing the thinnest insulation available to reduce wire harness diameter
Matching the insulation's temperature rating, chemical resistance, and abrasion resistance to the installation environment
Using the same insulation type throughout the aircraft for maintenance simplicity
blocks.feedback: Insulation must match the environment in three ways: temperature rating (for the local heat), chemical resistance (for fluids present), and abrasion resistance (for routing conditions). Failure in any one of these leads to insulation breakdown.

blocks.question: What is the key precaution when using automatic wire strippers on PTFE (Teflon) insulated wire?
choices: Heat the wire first to soften the insulation before using automatic strippers
Apply lubricant to the blade to reduce friction and prevent insulation tearing
Always use manual strippers for Teflon wire — automatic strippers cannot handle PTFE insulation
Verify the blade depth is correctly set for the wire gauge to avoid nicking the conductor strands
blocks.feedback: PTFE insulation is thin — blade depth must be exact. Too deep nicks the conductor; nicked strands create a stress concentration and will break under vibration. Correct blade depth for the gauge is essential.
